questions.prompt: Karim says: "I quite like the piano, but I'm crazy about the guitar." What is he telling you?

options.text: He likes the guitar much more.
He has only just begun to play the guitar.

questions.explanation: To be crazy about something — like to be mad about it — means to like it enormously, so the guitar comes well ahead of the piano, which he only quite likes. Neither "crazy" nor "mad" carries any anger or any madness inside these expressions, and nothing in the sentence says when he started playing. English grades a taste finely: "quite like" is mild approval, "like very much" is strong, and "crazy about" is the top of the ladder.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The gate closes ten minutes before take-off, so Tina ___."
questions.explanation: A modal is followed by the base form of the verb and by nothing else: must hurry. It takes no -s in the third person, however singular the subject is; it refuses the "to" of the infinitive; and it never takes an -ing form. The same three rules govern can, can't and mustn't — she can sing, he mustn't be late.

questions.prompt: A song tells of a boy who leaves his village for the city, fails twice, and comes home to open a workshop of his own. The same three words close every verse: keep on walking. Which sentence gives the MESSAGE of the song rather than its topic?

options.text: A boy leaves his village to work in the city.
Life in a big city is hard on young people.
Never stop, however often you fail.
The boy ends up opening his own workshop.

questions.explanation: The topic is what a song talks about — a boy, a village, a city — while the message is what it asks you to believe or to do once it is over. Here the words that come back at the end of every verse say it out loud: never stop, however often you fail. The departure and the workshop are the story itself, and the hardness of city life is something the story shows on the way, not what the song asks of you. When you hunt for a message, listen to what comes back and to the last lines.

questions.prompt: Which of these words contains the vowel sound of "home"?
questions.explanation: Close is built on the o…e group, so it carries the [ou] of home — the sound also heard in road, only and grow. The three others carry the [ei] of name: praise and chain spell it "ai", and stage spells it with the a…e group. Reading a vowel off the page means reading the letters as a group — o, oa, ow and o…e for [ou]; ai, ay, a…e and ei for [ei] — never letter by letter.

questions.prompt: A critic writes: "Her vocal ___ silenced a hall of three thousand people." Which word says great skill at doing something?
questions.explanation: Prowess names great skill at doing something, so vocal prowess is a singer's mastery of her own voice. Stardom is the state of being famous as a performer and renown is fame itself: both say that people know her, not that she sings well — and a young singer can have the skill long before either. Sorrow is deep sadness, which has no place in a sentence about technique.
